# litesearch


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

> Reading this on GitHub? The formatted
> [documentation](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/) is easier to
> read.

litesearch adds search to an application without a search server. Your
documents, their indexes and their vectors live in one SQLite file. Each
query runs a keyword search and a vector search, and litesearch merges
the two result lists.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>search</th>
<th>how it finds rows</th>
<th>good at</th>
<th>weak at</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>keyword</td>
<td>SQLite’s FTS5 extension keeps a full-text index: for each word, the
rows that hold it. bm25 ranks the rows. A row scores higher when it
holds the query’s words often and when those words are rare.</td>
<td>names, error codes, identifiers</td>
<td>the same idea in other words</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>vector</td>
<td>An encoder (an embedding model) turns text into an embedding, a list
of a few hundred numbers. Texts with similar meanings get embeddings
that are close together.</td>
<td>“ending a membership” for “cancel my subscription”</td>
<td>exact names</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges the two lists. A row gets 1/(60 +
its position) from each list that holds it, and the amounts add up. RRF
uses positions only. It never compares a bm25 score with a vector
distance, and it has no setting to tune.

There are two ways to use the library.

Start with
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index).
`Index.db` is the database under it. Use it when you need SQL against
the same data.

## Install

``` python
# usearch's SQLite extension is fetched, probed and configured on first use (see litesearch.postfix)
!uv add litesearch
```

litesearch has no optional extras. `rerank=True` needs `flashrank`. The
ONNX encoder
[`FastEncode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#fastencode)
needs `onnxruntime`. litesearch imports each one only when you use it,
and the error names the package to install.

## Route 1: [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)

An [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) is
a searchable collection. `add` puts files, folders or text into it.
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) cuts
each document into chunks of about 512 bytes and stores each chunk with
its embedding. `search` returns the chunks that best match a query.

Other methods work on whole documents and sections. `sections` ranks
sections, `read` returns the full text of one section, `toc` lists the
index as a table of contents, and `context` collects the best sections
for a query, for a language model.

``` python
ix = Index()                                        # pass a path to keep it on disk
ix.add('pdfs/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf')
hits = ix.search('how does multi-head attention work', limit=3)
[(h['heading'], h['page']) for h in hits]
```

Every hit has a `heading` and a `node_id`. During `add`,
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) builds
a document tree from the headings. The document is the root, its
chapters and sections are the nodes, and each chunk records its node.
`heading` is the path of headings above the chunk, such as
`attention is all you need › Abstract`. `node_id` is the document id,
`#`, and the section number. A hit tells you which section matched, not
only which 512 bytes.

``` python
sec = ix.sections('how does multi-head attention work', limit=2)   # ranked *sections*, not chunks
[(s['node_id'], (s['snippets'] or [''])[0][:60]) for s in sec]
```

``` python
ix.read(sec[0]['node_id'])['text'][:300]            # one whole section, reassembled
```

``` python
ix.toc(summaries=False)                             # the corpus — no embeddings computed at all
```

You decide one setting. `rerank=True` gives the top 30 candidates to a
cross-encoder from flashrank. A cross-encoder is a small model that
reads the query and each candidate together and scores the match. In the
evaluation it improved weighted MRR by 0.026 to 0.077, in all twelve
measured cells. It makes a query about 10 times slower and downloads a 4
MB model on first use.

``` python
ix.search('how does multi-head attention work', rerank=True)
```

For source code, use `add_code`. It cuts Python files at top-level
functions and classes with Python’s own parser. Code chunks get no
document tree, so `toc`, `sections` and `read` do not cover them:

``` python
ix.add_code('litesearch')      # a folder, or the name of an installed package
```

## Route 2: [`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)

[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
opens a SQLite database and returns a
[fastlite](https://fastlite.answer.ai/) `Database`. fastlite is a thin
layer over SQLite that gives each table a Python object. The first
vector search loads usearch’s SQLite extension into the connection,
which adds vector distance functions you can call from SQL.
`db.usearch_sql()` loads it before that, for SQL of your own. Pass a
file path to keep the database on disk, or nothing for one held in
memory.

The cell below does by hand what
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) does.
It loads an encoder and creates a store: a table with a text column, an
embedding column and a full-text index. Then it embeds five sentences
and searches them.

Tell the search the number type of the stored vectors. An embedding is
stored as raw bytes. litesearch assumes float16, which is half the size
of float32. The static encoder returns float32, so the code converts to
float16 before it stores. If you store float32 and search as float16,
every distance comes back empty, litesearch prints a warning, and the
vector search returns rows in table order.

``` python
db    = database()
enc   = static_embedder()             # model2vec: no GPU, no ONNX runtime
store = db.get_store(hash=True, ann=True)
emb   = lambda xs: np.asarray(enc.encode(list(xs)), dtype=np.float16)   # a store holds float16

texts = ['attention mechanisms in neural networks', 'transformer architecture for sequences',
         'stochastic gradient descent and learning rate schedules',
         'positional encoding and token embeddings', 'dropout reduces overfitting']
store.insert_all([dict(content=t, embedding=e.tobytes()) for t, e in zip(texts, emb(texts))],
                 upsert=True, hash_id='id', hash_id_columns=['content'])
store.rebuild_index()

q = 'self-attention mechanism'
db.search(q, emb([q])[0].tobytes(), columns=['content'], limit=2)
```

## What is under [`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)

[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
returns a fastlite `Database`. Four packages sit under it, and each one
has one job.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>package</th>
<th>its job in litesearch</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><a href="https://github.com/rogerbinns/apsw">apsw</a></td>
<td>the SQLite driver. It holds the connection, registers the Python
FTS5 tokenizers and loads extensions.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/apswutils">apswutils</a></td>
<td>the table layer over apsw. It creates tables, adds columns, inserts
and upserts rows, turns on FTS5 with its triggers, and writes the SQL of
a full-text search.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><a href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/fastlite">fastlite</a></td>
<td>the <code>Database</code> object you use: <code>db.t.name</code> for
a table, <code>db.q(sql)</code> for a query</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><a href="https://github.com/vedicreader/adhara">adhara</a></td>
<td>a SQLite extension in Rust: a native tokenizer, and an exact vector
search on all cores</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

litesearch adds the stores, the tokenizers, the search functions and the
thread safety. Your code calls litesearch and fastlite. It does not call
apsw, apswutils or adhara directly.

### adhara

[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
loads adhara into each connection when adhara is installed. adhara is a
dependency of litesearch on Linux and macOS. It has no Windows wheel, so
on Windows litesearch works as before. If adhara does not load,
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
gives a warning and the search runs in Python.

No function signature changes. A search returns the same rows in the
same order with or without adhara. These behaviours are new:

- `vec_search`, the exact vector search, asks adhara for the rowids of
  the nearest rows. adhara compares the query with every vector in
  memory, on all cores. `vec_search` then reads only those rows in SQL
  and computes `_dist` as before.
  [`Database.search`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database.search)
  calls `vec_search` when `ann=False` or when `where` is set.
- `vec_search` does not use adhara for a search with `offset`,
  `where_args`, an embedding column other than `embedding`, the
  `divergence` metric or `float64` vectors.
- Rows at the same distance come in rowid order. Before, their order
  depended on the SQLite query plan.
- `SANSKRIT_TOKENIZE` is `'adhara'`, the native form of the cross-script
  tokenizer. Use it for a new FTS table. A table made with `'sanskrit'`
  keeps working.
- Each connection has the SQL table function `adhara_hybrid`. It runs a
  keyword search, a vector search and RRF in one call. The adhara README
  documents it.

The HNSW search (`ann=True` with no `where`) and the keyword search do
not use adhara. New stores keep the tokenizer chain
`porter simplify casefold 1 sanskrit unicodewords`. A Swift app can read
these stores with adhara’s Swift package.

The table shows `Vault.search` from
[vishalakshi](https://github.com/vedicreader/vishalakshi), which is
built on
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index). The
vault holds 181,290 chunks, on a 14-core arm64 Mac. Each time is for 10
searches. The hits were the same with and without adhara.

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>search</th>
<th>without adhara</th>
<th>with adhara</th>
</tr>
</thead>

<tr>
<td>no <code>where</code>: HNSW</td>
<td>51 ms</td>

</tr>
<tr>

<td>518 ms</td>

A `where` that few rows pass is slower with adhara. SQLite reads only
the matching rows through an index, and adhara compares the query with
every vector.

## Threads: share one connection, or give each thread its own

A SQLite connection used from several threads needs care.
`database(shared=True)` wraps the connection so that threads can share
it. Each statement runs alone, and a thread that opens a transaction
keeps the connection until it commits. Without `shared=True`, give each
thread its own
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
on the same file. SQLite’s WAL mode, which litesearch turns on, lets
those connections read while another writes.

`python -m evals.shared_conn` measures both on a store of 20,000 rows
with an HNSW index, on a 14-core arm64 Mac:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>shared</th>
<th>one each</th>
<th>one each, memstatus off</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>FTS queries/s, 8 threads</td>
<td>608</td>
<td>441</td>
<td>6,820</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>brute-force vector scans/s, 8 threads</td>
<td>70</td>
<td>176</td>
<td>168</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>HNSW queries/s, 8 threads</td>
<td>4,705</td>
<td>2,748</td>
<td>2,587</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTS p50 / p99, 4 readers beside a writer</td>
<td>106 / 193 ms</td>
<td>13.4 / 33.0 ms</td>
<td>1.6 / 3.4 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>resident memory, HNSW index loaded</td>
<td>17 MB</td>
<td>17 MB per thread</td>
<td>17 MB per thread</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

By default SQLite counts every memory allocation under one lock for the
whole process. Threads on separate connections then wait for each other.
Run
`apsw.shutdown(); apsw.config(apsw.SQLITE_CONFIG_MEMSTATUS, 0); apsw.initialize()`
before the first connection opens to turn the counting off. After that,
`apsw.memory_used()` returns 0. litesearch does not do this, because it
changes the whole process.

Share one connection when your threads share one database object and
writes are short. For parallel reads, or a steady writer, give each
thread its own connection and turn the counting off. `evals/RESULTS.md`
has the method and the results for every thread count.

## What the evaluation says

The defaults come from `evals/`. It runs 120 known-item queries for each
of three corpora: EU legislation, arXiv papers and a 19th-century
astrology treatise. A known-item query is written to find one passage.
The score is MRR (mean reciprocal rank): 1 if the right section is
first, 1/2 if second, and so on. Three quarters of the weight is on
queries that do not copy the words of the answer.
`python -m evals.decide` gives every number.

The changes above the blank row are on by default. The changes below it
are off.

The choice of encoder matters little: across four encoders the spread is
0.018 to 0.046. The default, `potion-multilingual-128M`, is a static
model. It looks up one vector for each token, and it indexes about 1,700
times more cheaply than a neural encoder.

The document tree does not improve ranking. It does help a language
model: on a Sanskrit corpus, `context()` raises verse-level recall from
0.190 to 0.340.

On this benchmark, keyword search alone beats hybrid search, because
each query rewords words from its target. On `evals/multihop.py`, where
the answer shares no word with the question, keyword search finds
nothing, and vector search puts the target first in 53% to 84% of
queries.

Three related jobs are in other packages.
[pdflite](https://github.com/vedicreader/pdflite) reads PDFs.
[ganapati](https://github.com/vedicreader/ganapati) handles Sanskrit
metre, verse chunking and lemmas.
[vruksha](https://github.com/vedicreader/vruksha) builds an entity
graph.

Every store matches words across scripts. A tokenizer is the part of
FTS5 that splits text into the words it indexes. litesearch’s tokenizer
adds a copy of each word in plain ASCII letters, so `श्रीमाता`, `śrīmātā`
and `srimata` reach the same row. It also adds a looser copy that
follows English spelling, so `Bheeshma` reaches `भीष्म` and `Bhīṣma`.
English words keep their own entries. The looser copy makes the index
14.7% larger. With it, a Devanagari query found the right verse every
time (recall 1.000) with every encoder tested. A connection that has not
registered the tokenizer cannot search the store. That includes the
`sqlite3` command-line tool. Open the store with
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database).
